abstract: |
  Middle Palaeolithic assemblages vary widely in technology, and whether that variability reflects separate cultural traditions or shared responses to environmental pressures is a long-standing question in the study of human evolution. Among the most distinctive of these technologies is Quina, a specific technological behaviour built around thick, asymmetric blanks and the prolonged resharpening and recycling of the tools made on them, and long understood as an adaptation to high mobility in open, seasonally structured environments. In Europe, where it has been studied for over a century, Quina documented within a narrow glacial interval; in the eastern Old World it was, until recently, unknown. The identification of a complete Quina system at Longtan, on the southeastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau, changed this, but rested on a single case. Here we show that Longtan is not an isolated occurrence but one instance of a regional practice. Analysing Quina scrapers and resharpening flakes surface collected across two basins, and testing them against the Longtan material, we find that they share the same technological concept and the same strong preference for a single raw material, without systematic variation across the landscape; we term this regional entity the Quina Valley. Its setting, a dry-hot valley on the plateau margin, is far removed from the cold, open landscapes of the European Quina, yet poses an ecological problem of the same structure, one of patchy, seasonally organised resources reached by moving through the terrain. The significance of this study lies not only in identifying a regional Quina entity on the eastern side of the Old World, but also in providing an environmental rationale for its emergence in this region. Future excavation, by recovering absolute ages and faunal remains, will be essential to building a regional chronological framework, identifying the people behind this technology and reconstructing the subsistence strategies it served.

# Introduction

The Middle Palaeolithic (\~300-40 ka) was a period of marked diversity in both hominin populations and lithic technology, and what produced that diversity has been contested since Bordes read the variability of Mousterian assemblages as the signature of distinct cultural traditions [@bordesMousterianCulturesFrance1961; @bordes1950]. The same variability has since been attributed to the activities carried out at a site [@binfordbinford1966], to change through time [@mellars1969], to the raw material available locally and the distances over which it was moved [@geneste1985; @kuhn1995], and to the degree to which tools had been reduced [@dibble1987]. The Quina Mousterian has been central to that debate.

The Quina Mousterian is one of the best-defined Middle Palaeolithic techno-complexes [@delagnes2006; @faivre2017], and what distinguishes it is not a tool type but a techno-economic system, the Quina system, whose defining features form three interlocking dimensions [@delpiano2022; @peresani2023]. The first dimension is blank production. Quina cores receive little preparation and are reduced through alternating, concatenated removals on sub-parallel and secant surfaces, with invasive detachments that optimise the volume of stone converted into blanks [@turq1989; @turq2000; @Bourguignon1997]. The target product is a thick flake, asymmetric in cross-section, with a sharp cutting edge on one margin and a thick, often cortical, back opposite [@turq1992; @hiscock2009]. This asymmetry is what allows such a tool to be repeatedly resharpened [@turq1992; @hiscock2009]. The second dimension is edge maintenance, achieved through Quina retouch. Here the working edge is not merely produced but sustained, and resharpening follows a regular rhythm [@lemoriniScrapersLifeHistory2016; @Bourguignon1997]. Early episodes detach relatively large resharpening flakes and leave convex scars, giving a plano-convex edge and preserving volume for later work; as retouch proceeds it concentrates on the margin itself, producing smaller concave scars with stepped or hinged terminations and a plano-concave edge that keeps the tool serviceable. Each generation of retouch therefore restores a working edge without drawing on new raw material. The third dimension is ramification of the reduction sequence [@bourguignonRAMIFICATIONCHAINESOPERATOIRES; @faivre2017]. Resharpening flakes detached during edge maintenance carry cutting edges of their own and can be used directly, as use-wear analysis has shown [@claud2012]; in some cases they were themselves retouched into tools [@ruanQuinaLithicTechnology2025a]. Quina flakes, besides being shaped into Quina scrapers, are thick enough to serve as cores for small flakes (i.e. core-on-flake) [@hiscock2009]. Use-wear on scrapers and resharpening flakes from the same assemblages indicates that the two were put to different tasks, scraping and cutting respectively [@delpiano2022], so that ramification widened the functional range of the toolkit as well as extending its life. Efficient blank production, intensive edge maintenance and ramification together create an economy of stone use in which the thick Quina flake functions as a transportable and highly extendable package of raw material, yielding a large amount of working edge from a small initial investment [@hiscock2009; @delpiano2022].

Quina technology has been interpreted as an adaptation to high mobility in open environments where resources were patchily distributed and seasonally structured, and this interpretation rests on three lines of evidence. Faunal assemblages from Quina sites are typically dominated by a single gregarious and migratory species, most often reindeer, although equids and bovids predominate in some regions [@delpechLenvironnementAnimalMousteriens1996; @delagnesShiftsNeandertalMobility2011; @delpiano2022; @castelNeandertalSubsistenceStrategies2017]. Settlement organisation is correspondingly structured, with residential camps surrounded by task-specific satellite locations given over to hunting and carcass processing [@delagnesShiftsNeandertalMobility2011]. At the landscape scale, Quina assemblages occur in open, lightly wooded settings in which prey were distributed across the terrain in a way that was patchy but not random [@delpechLenvironnementAnimalMousteriens1996; @hiscock2009]. Foragers under these conditions are argued to have relied on seasonal, high-mobility strategies of resource use and tool provisioning [@hiscock2009; @delagnesShiftsNeandertalMobility2011; @castelNeandertalSubsistenceStrategies2017], and it is here that the technological economy described above becomes advantageous: versatile blanks, tools with long use-lives and cores requiring little preparation together lower the time and energy costs of replacing equipment on the move, and reduce the risk both of being left without an effective cutting edge far from a source of raw material and of carrying a toolkit ill-suited to the tasks that a given season and location happened to present [@hiscock2009; @delagnesShiftsNeandertalMobility2011].

The distinction between the Quina system and Quina retouch alone matters when its distribution is assessed. In the strict sense, with blank production, edge maintenance and ramification operating together, Quina system is documented in western and southern Europe within a narrow interval between MIS 4 and early MIS 3, coinciding with pronounced global climatic instability [@delagnesShiftsNeandertalMobility2011; @delpiano2022]. Quina retouch taken on its own is far more widely distributed: in the Levant it has been reported in Acheulo–Yabrudian industries dating from as early as MIS 11 [@agamInterpretingQuinaDemiQuina2020; @FALGUERES2022101266; @zaidnerEndLowerPaleolithic2016]. The occurrence of so distinctive a way of maintaining a working edge in contexts this widely separated in time and space raises the possibility that Quina retouch is a recurrent solution to a recurrent problem rather than the signature of a single tradition. Neither the system nor Quina retouch, however, had been securely documented in the East Asia.

Whether East Asia has a Middle Palaeolithic has long been contested. On the conventional view, substantial innovation in lithic technology was deferred until the Upper Palaeolithic, leaving no phase corresponding to the western Middle Palaeolithic [@gaoPaleolithicCulturesChina2013; @nortonEastAsianMiddle2009]. Recent discoveries have provided new evidence that is reshaping this long-standing understanding. Discoid technology is documented at Lingjing (\~125–90 ka) [@liTechnologicalBehaviorEarly2019; @zhaoEarliestCentripetalFlaking2026], and Levallois technology at Guanyindong (\~170–80 ka) [@huLateMiddlePleistocene2019] and Jinsitai (\~47–37 ka) [@liEasternmostMiddlePaleolithic2018]. These finds indicate that the technological scenario of the East Asian Middle Palaeolithic is more complex than the conventional view allows. It is against this background that we identified a complete Quina system at Longtan, dated to \~60–50 ka [@ruanQuinaLithicTechnology2025a], the first Quina site in East Asia to be unambiguously characterised, formally excavated, securely dated and systematically analysed. This discovery not only filled a long-standing gap in the eastern Old World distribution of Quina technology, but also provided new evidence for reassessing the diversity and complexity of the East Asian Middle Palaeolithic. More importantly, Longtan is unlikely to be an isolated case. Surface collections bearing Quina features have been recovered from river terraces at a number of localities in the Huangping Basin, where Longtan is situated, and in the neighbouring Binchuan Basin [@ruanQuinaLithicTechnology2025a; @xiao2024a2022]. These finds suggest that Quina technology on the southeastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau may not be confined to a single site, but may instead represent a regional technological phenomenon of some spatial extent.

The Huangping and Binchuan basins lie in the Hengduan Mountains, on the southeastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau, in what is today the dry-hot valley zone of the Jinsha River drainage. At roughly 26°N, in relief of this amplitude and under monsoon control [@xiaoVariationSouthwestMonsoon2010; @zhishengGlacialInterglacialIndianSummer2011], the region is governed by a climatic regime unlike the mid-latitude, glacial-stage settings of western Europe in which the European Quina is documented [@delpiano2022; @delpechLenvironnementAnimalMousteriens1996]. A technology usually associated with open landscapes, seasonally structured resources and high mobility subsistence therefore occurs here under a quite different climatic regime, and whether the two settings nonetheless resemble one another in the respects that bear on how technology was organised is a question we return to once the technological results are in place. All of the localities so far identified, moreover, apart from Longtan itself, are surface collections without absolute dates, so that whether they constitute a coherent regional technological entity is equally open.

The analysis proceeds in two steps. We ask first whether the surface collections share a consistent technological concept with the Quina technology at Longtan, and can therefore be identified as a single regional technological entity, which we term the Quina Valley. To answer this we systematically analyse the most diagnostic elements of the Quina system, the Quina scrapers and the resharpening flakes removed in maintaining them, and assess their technological consistency with the excavated material from Longtan. Only if the first step can be sustained does the second question arise: whether such an entity can be accounted for by the environmental setting of the region, its available resources and the strategies by which technology was organised. Here we bring together the spatial distribution of the localities, the raw materials used at them and the environmental characteristics of the region. Taken together, these analyses clarify the regional distribution of Quina technology in East Asia and provide new insight into the relationship between environmental constraints, technological convergence and regional technological organisation during the Middle Palaeolithic.

# Regional Geological and Palaeoenvironmental Setting

The tectonic framework of the study area determines both where its intermontane basins lie and where knappable stone is available within them. The area falls within the Jinsha River drainage in the southern Hengduan Mountains, on the southeastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau, and is controlled by a system of approximately north–south trending faults: continued relative uplift of massifs such as Yulong Mountains and Diancang Shan, alternating with subsidence of the ground between them, has produced a series of north–south trending intermontane basins, among them Lijiang, Heqing and Dali \[Li et al. 2014; An et al. 2011\]. The two basins considered here, Huangping and Binchuan, lie within this same system. This alternation of uplifted ranges and downfaulted basins, combined with the Indian monsoon and the warm, moist airflow from the southwest, gives the deeply incised valley floors a dry-hot valley climate, sheltered from precipitation by the surrounding relief and marked by a sharp division between wet and dry seasons and by high insolation; the modern vegetation there is dominated by drought-tolerant shrub and savanna formations \[\]. The Quina localities discussed here are concentrated in two of these basins, the Huangping Basin in the southwest of Heqing County and the neighbouring Binchuan Basin, each of them cut by tributaries of the Jinsha River: the Caifeng River in the Huangping Basin, and the Sangyuan River together with its tributary the Liandong River in the Binchuan Basin. The two basins differ in bedrock. Permian volcanic rocks are extensively exposed along the western side of the Huangping Basin, with Triassic sedimentary rocks predominating to the east, whereas the Binchuan Basin is largely mantled by unconsolidated Quaternary sediments and exposes its Permian volcanic basement only locally. The volcanic sequence comprises basalt, tuff and trachyte. Because the rivers of both basins cut across these outcrops, volcanic cobbles were carried into the gravel bars of the valley floors, and it was these bars, rather than the outcrops themselves, that supplied the stone used at the localities.

The regional monsoon record places the occupation of these basins within an interval of recurrent aridity rather than within a settled climatic phase. The nearest palaeoclimate records covering this period come from the lacustrine sediments of the Heqing Basin, about 60 km north of the Huangping and Binchuan basins and some 650 m higher, which are among the longest and most continuous environmental sequences available for the Asian monsoon domain and are highly sensitive to variation in the Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM) \[Xiao et al. 2010; An et al. 2011\]. Magnetic and geochemical proxies there record a return to aridity between 69 and 57 ka, corresponding to MIS 4, and a generally humid MIS 3 thereafter, punctuated by repeated arid events \[Yang et al. 2025\]; millennial-scale weakenings of the monsoon, corresponding closely to North Atlantic cold events, have been resolved in the same basin from 52 ka onwards \[Hou et al. 2026\], overlapping the end of the interval dated at Longtan and continuing after it. Given the distance and altitudinal offset just noted, these records register monsoon variation at a regional scale rather than local conditions at any one place, and we treat them here as context rather than as a proxy for the localities themselves. Read at that scale, what matters is not whether a particular stage was on balance wetter or drier, but that the occupation falls where the MIS 4 arid phase gives way to a monsoon recovery that was itself repeatedly interrupted.

Longtan provides the local counterpart to this regional picture, since it preserves both a secure chronology and a record of vegetation change. Optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dating places its in situ cultural layer at \~60–50 ka [@ruanQuinaLithicTechnology2025a], and Longtan remains the only locality in the study area with an age determination of this kind. The nearby Tianhuadong site, where material of this kind has also been reported, has yielded OSL ages of \~90–40 ka for its cultural layers \[\], but it has not been systematically analysed, and neither its chronology nor its technological attribution is yet secure enough to carry weight here. The surface collections examined below have no independent age control, and none can be transferred to them by association: what the Longtan dates establish is when the Quina system was present in this landscape, not when any individual surface collection was formed. What Longtan adds beyond a date is a local environmental record. Pollen analysis there documents a transition from coniferous forest to a more open woodland-steppe, with the Quina-bearing layer falling within the phase of vegetation opening [@ruanQuinaLithicTechnology2025a]. Taken together, the two records indicate that people were present in this landscape while it was becoming more open locally, and during an interval when the regional monsoon system was subject to repeated interruption. Whether that setting can account for the technology found within it is a question we return to once the technological results have been presented.

# Materials and methods

## Survey and selection of localities

The surface material analysed here was recovered during four seasons of pedestrian survey in the Huangping and Binchuan basins, carried out in 2010, 2013, 2016 and 2022. Survey followed the main valleys of the two basins, the Caifeng River in the Huangping Basin and the Sangyuan River together with its tributary the Liandong River in the Binchuan Basin, and each flight of river terraces was walked in turn. Survey areas and walking routes were designed to cover the full range of landforms that humans might have used in the past. Routes were recorded continuously using the mobile GPS application 2bulu, localities and artefacts were photographed, and a field form was completed for each locality giving its position, its place within the terrace sequence, its straight-line distance to the river channel, and the number and types of artefacts present.

Because this study is concerned with Quina technology, the localities recorded during survey were then screened, and only those yielding diagnostic Quina scrapers and resharpening flakes were retained. On this criterion, 22 of the 33 localities recorded in the Binchuan Basin (67%) and all five of those recorded in the Huangping Basin contain Quina specimens (@tbl-localities). Two consequences of this design should be stated at the outset. First, the criterion is one of presence rather than of degree: localities were retained on whether Quina pieces occur at them, not on how those pieces were made or how far they had been reduced, so that none of the technological variables analysed below entered the selection. Second, what Section 4 reports are patterns among Quina-bearing localities rather than a map of Quina technology across the two basins; since the visibility of surface localities depends on exposure, vegetation cover and survey intensity, these patterns are read here as trends and not as reality densities.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-localities
#| tbl-cap: "The Quina-bearing localities retained for analysis, by basin and valley. Landform is the position within the terrace sequence, T2 the lowest terrace, with the three localities standing well above that sequence entered as hilltops. Coordinates are degrees, minutes and seconds, and elevation is metres above sea level. The last two columns give the assemblage on which the analyses below are based."

# decimal degrees -> d m s, rounding to a tenth of a second before splitting the
# parts, so that a second rounding up to 60 cannot appear in the output
dms <- function(x, hemi) {
  tot <- round(x * 3600, 1)
  d   <- floor(tot / 3600)
  m   <- floor((tot - d * 3600) / 60)
  s   <- tot - d * 3600 - m * 60
  sprintf("%d°%02d′%04.1f″%s", d, m, s, hemi)
}

# read here rather than from the results chunk: this table falls earlier in the
# document, so the analysis objects do not exist yet
sites_tbl <- read_excel(here("data", "Site_information.xlsx"))
names(sites_tbl) <- trimws(names(sites_tbl))
sites_tbl <- sites_tbl |>
  transmute(name = gsub("_", " ", trimws(as.character(name))),
            # the data file names this basin after the county, the text after the basin
            basin = ifelse(grepl("^Heqing", trimws(basin)), "Huangping Basin", "Binchuan Basin"),
            valley = trimws(as.character(river_ID)),
            geomorph = trimws(as.character(geomorph)),
            lat = as.numeric(lat), lon = as.numeric(lon), elev = as.numeric(elev_m),
            n_sc = as.integer(n_Quina_scraper), n_rf = as.integer(n_Resharpening_flake))

loc_fmt <- bind_rows(lapply(c("Binchuan Basin", "Huangping Basin"), function(b) {
  s <- sites_tbl[sites_tbl$basin == b, ]
  bind_rows(
    data.frame(Locality = sprintf("**%s** (*n* = %d localities)", b, nrow(s)),
               valley = "", geomorph = "", lat = "", lon = "", elev = "",
               n_sc = as.character(sum(s$n_sc)), n_rf = as.character(sum(s$n_rf))),
    data.frame(Locality = paste0(IND, s$name), valley = s$valley, geomorph = s$geomorph,
               lat = dms(s$lat, "N"), lon = dms(s$lon, "E"), elev = as.character(s$elev),
               n_sc = as.character(s$n_sc), n_rf = as.character(s$n_rf)))
})) |>
  bind_rows(data.frame(Locality = "**Total**", valley = "", geomorph = "",
                       lat = "", lon = "", elev = "",
                       n_sc = as.character(sum(sites_tbl$n_sc)),
                       n_rf = as.character(sum(sites_tbl$n_rf))))

knitr::kable(loc_fmt, row.names = FALSE,
             align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
             col.names = c("Locality", "Valley", "Landform", "Latitude",
                           "Longitude", "Elevation (m)", "Quina scrapers",
                           "Resharpening flakes"))
```

## Survey and analysis of raw materials

To establish what raw material was locally available, gravel bars were sampled at five points along three river channels. At each point an area of 1–2 m² was cleared and every cobble longer than 30 mm exposed at the surface was recorded. For each cobble we recorded length, width and thickness (mm), roundness on a four-point scale (0–3, from least to most rounded) and shape (sub-oval, tabular or irregular). These records give the relative abundance of each lithology on the gravel bars.

To characterise the internal properties of the dominant raw material, thin sections were prepared from five trachyte cobbles and examined petrographically, with mineral composition determined by energy-dispersive spectroscopy. Identifications were carried out by the Guangxi Institute of Geological Survey and the China University of Geosciences (Wuhan). The raw material of each artefact was assigned macroscopically to the same lithological categories, using the surveyed cobbles as a reference collection.

Differences in raw material composition, both between the gravel bars and the artefacts and between spatial units, were tested by permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA), stratified at two scales, basin and valley.

Because the artefacts are made overwhelmingly on river cobbles, the straight-line distance from each locality to the nearest channel was used as a proxy for proximity to a source of raw material. These distances are strongly skewed, the groups differ considerably in size, and their variances are unequal, so differences between the two basins were tested with a Mann–Whitney U test and differences among the three valleys with a Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test; medians are reported as the measure of central tendency and the rank tests taken as the primary criterion. Cobble size was summarised as the geometric mean of length, width and thickness and compared between lithologies with a Mann–Whitney U test [@erenRoleRawMaterial2014].

Raw material selection was quantified with Jacobs' electivity index *D* [@jacobs1974], a modification of Ivlev's index that corrects for the relative abundance of the available resources:

$$D = \frac{r - p}{\,r + p - 2\,r\,p\,}$$

where *r* is the proportion of a given raw material among the artefacts and *p* is its proportion among the cobbles recorded in the gravel survey. *D* ranges from −1 (complete avoidance) through 0 (use in proportion to availability) to +1 (complete selection). It was computed for each raw material in the surface Quina scrapers against availability pooled across the gravel survey. Materials present among the artefacts but absent from the survey take *D* = +1 and are read as evidence of non-local procurement; materials present in the survey but absent from the artefacts take *D* = −1.

## Techno-typological analysis of Quina retouch products

The techno-typological observations and measurements follow established practice in the study of Quina technology [@Bourguignon1997; @peresani2023; @ruanQuinaLithicTechnology2025a; @hiscockConstructionMorphologicalDiversity2008]. For each scraper we recorded length, width, thickness and mass; blank type; cortex position; platform type and platform depth (PD); interior platform angle (IPA); the number of retouch generations; the numbers of convex scars and concave scars; the geometric index of unifacial reduction (GIUR) [@kuhnGeometricIndexReduction1990] and the proportion of the perimeter retouched; the edge angle; and its attribution within Bordes' type list [@bordes1961; @debenath1994]. For each resharpening flake we recorded platform type, PD, IPA and exterior platform angle (EPA). Statistical tests were chosen according to the type of each variable and the distribution of the data, with parametric or non-parametric procedures used depending on whether the data approximated normality [@Zar1999]. Relationships between edge angle and GIUR, the proportion of retouched edge and the mean number of retouch generations were examined with Spearman rank correlation, with p-values adjusted by the Bonferroni procedure. The difference between the EPAs of the resharpening flakes and the edge angles of the scrapers was tested with Welch's t-test, so that unequal variances would not affect the inference [@Welch1947].

To test the technological consistency between the surface Quina scrapers and the excavated material, the Quina scrapers from Longtan were used as the reference, and non-Quina scrapers from the same site were included as a technological control group. To reduce dimensionality and minimise redundancy among correlated variables, six of the recorded variables were selected for multivariate analysis as the most representative: thickness, proportion of the perimeter retouched, GIUR, number of total scars, number of retouch generations and edge angle. All were standardised to z-scores and differences between specimens computed as Euclidean distances. Differences between groups were tested by PERMANOVA, with the proportion of variance explained (*R*²) reported for each pairwise comparison. The non-Quina scrapers serve to calibrate the scale on which those *R*² values are read: if the same set of variables separates Quina from ordinary scrapers with a high *R*² while the two Quina groups differ only at a low *R*², the latter is more likely to reflect a real technological similarity than a lack of statistical power. At the univariate level, mean GIUR, scar count and mean number of retouch generations were compared with Kruskal–Wallis rank sum tests followed by Dunn's post hoc comparisons, and thickness, proportion of the perimeter retouched and edge angle with Welch's ANOVA followed by Welch's t post hoc comparisons; all post hoc comparisons were corrected using the Bonferroni method. Technological dispersion between groups was tested with PERMDISP. To compare the degree of variation within groups, the coefficients of variation (CV) of length, width, thickness, mass and edge angle were tested for equality across groups using the Krishnamoorthy–Lee modified signed likelihood ratio test (KL-MSLRT) [@krishnamoorthy2014], these being ratio-scale variables with a true zero. GIUR, the proportion of the perimeter retouched, number of total scars and the number of retouch generations were instead compared with Fligner–Killeen tests: the first two are bounded on \[0, 1\], which leaves the CV without a clear interpretation, and the last two are counts whose variance structure does not meet the assumptions required for comparing CVs. To assess how robust the results are, the analyses were repeated with the surface specimens collected from within the area of the Longtan site removed.

To test whether technological variation is systematically structured by the landscape, the analysis was repeated with the locality as the unit, each locality represented by the median value of its Quina scrapers on the same six variables. Four landscape variables were considered: basin (Huangping or Binchuan), the height of the locality above the present-day channel, distance from the locality to that channel, and assemblage size (number of specimens). Height above the channel was used in preference to a categorical terrace level, and in preference to absolute elevation: it is the continuous quantity of which terrace level is a discretisation, and because it is measured from the local channel rather than from sea level, the difference in base level between the two basins cancels out. Basin, the only categorical variable, was tested with PERMANOVA and PERMDISP; the three continuous variables with Spearman rank correlation, and with locality-level PERMANOVA on Euclidean distances.

All statistical analyses were carried out in R 4.5.2 [@rcoreteam2025]. Package versions, permutation, Monte Carlo and bootstrap settings, and the random seed are given in Supplementary S1.

## Reproducibility and open materials

Computational reproducibility remains a challenge in archaeological science, yet it underpins both the credibility of quantitative results and their re-use by others [@marwickComputationalReproducibilityArchaeological2017; @marwickOpenScienceArchaeology2017]. All materials needed to reproduce the analyses reported here are therefore available in a version-controlled online repository at \[\[OSF DOI\]\]. These comprise the raw data underlying every reported result together with the complete code used for the analyses and for the figures derived from them. The repository is organised with a logical folder structure and relative file paths, so that the code runs without manual modification.

# Results

## Landscape distribution and raw material economy

Quina localities in both basins lie along the valley systems, on river terraces, and at consistently short distances from the channels. In the Huangping Basin they are concentrated on the second and third terraces; in the Binchuan Basin they extend across the second to fourth terraces (T2–T4), with a small number (*n* = 3) occurring higher, on hilltops. Because the artefacts are made overwhelmingly on river cobbles, the straight-line distance from a locality to the nearest channel serves as a proxy for ease of access to lithic raw material. Across the three valleys, the Sangyuan, Liandong and Caifeng, these distances are short and similarly distributed, with a median of `r f(dist_median, 0)` m. Neither comparison detected a difference between spatial units, whether at the scale of the basin (*U* = `r f(dist_basin_U, 0)`, *p* `r fp(dist_basin_p)`) or of the valley (*H* = `r f(dist_river_H, 2)`, *df* = `r dist_river_df`, *p* `r fp(dist_river_p)`). Access to river gravels therefore appears to have been broadly comparable across the study area, so that differences in the raw materials actually used at these localities are unlikely to be explained by differential proximity to a source.

Raw material use does not follow raw material abundance. On the gravel bars, sandstone is the most abundant lithology (`r f(sand_avail_pct, 1)`% of `r n_cobble` cobbles), with trachyte second (`r f(trach_avail_pct, 1)`%); among the artefacts, trachyte accounts for `r f(trach_used_pct, 1)`%. The bars are not uniform in composition, however: raw material composition differs significantly between sampling points (*R*² = `r f(cobbleLoc_v["R2"], 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(cobbleLoc_v["F"], 2)`, *p* `r fp(cobbleLoc_v["p"])`), and stratified analysis attributes this variation to differences between valleys (*R*² = `r f(cobbleRiver_v["R2"], 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(cobbleRiver_v["F"], 2)`, *p* `r fp(cobbleRiver_v["p"])`) rather than within them. Sandstone-dominated and trachyte-richer bars are therefore distributed unevenly across the study area, in a pattern that follows the contrast in bedrock described in Section 2 (\[\[Fig. X\]\]). If knappers had simply worked whatever lay most abundantly at hand, the raw material composition of the artefacts should vary from valley to valley in the same way.

That expectation is not met. The raw material composition of the Quina scrapers is uniform across the study area, differing neither between basins (*R*² = `r f(usedA_basin_v["R2"], 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(usedA_basin_v["F"], 2)`, *p* `r fp(usedA_basin_v["p"])`) nor between valleys (*R*² = `r f(usedA_river_v["R2"], 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(usedA_river_v["F"], 2)`, *p* `r fp(usedA_river_v["p"])`) (@fig-raw-material-composition). The same material was selected wherever knappers used, although sandstone is more abundant on the bars and although the composition of those bars varies from valley to valley. Jacobs' electivity index puts the strength of that preference on a common scale: trachyte is strongly selected (*D* = `r f(D_trach, 2)`) and sandstone strongly avoided (*D* = `r f(D_sand, 2)`), with quartz and mudstone likewise avoided (*D* = `r f(D_quartz, 2)` in each case, neither being used at all); andesite returns *D* = `r f(D_and, 2)`, but only because the `r andesite_n` andesite artefacts have no counterpart among the recorded cobbles, so that its index is undefined in practice rather than informative. Because D returns to zero only when a raw material is used in proportion to its availability, trachyte would have to make up some `r f(trach_used_pct, 0)`% of the gravel before its use could be read as neutral; no redistribution of availability among the valleys approaches that figure, so neither the direction nor the magnitude of the selection depends on how availability is pooled. The selection of trachyte, in other words, was made against local abundance rather than in step with it.

```{r}
#| label: fig-raw-material-composition
#| fig-cap: "aw material composition of river-bar cobbles and surface-collected Quina scrapers across the three valleys. Each row of stacked bars represents a 100% composition: the upper row shows the lithology of available river cobbles, and the lower row shows the lithology of surface-collected Quina scrapers. Per-cell sample sizes are indicated by bar charts on the right."
#| fig-width: 5.9
#| fig-height: 4.25

material_colors_fig <- c(Trachyte = "#E07C90", Sandstone = "#6BA8CE",
                         Quartz = "#E6C25C", Mudstone = "#9B87C4", Andesite = "#6FB98E")

fig_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E6E8EB", linewidth = 0.3),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),

        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#202124", size = 9),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#E8E8E8", color = NA),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8.5), legend.text = element_text(size = 8.5),
        legend.key = element_blank(), legend.key.size = unit(10, "pt"),
        plot.background = element_rect(color = NA, fill = "white"),
        panel.background = element_rect(color = NA, fill = "white"))

valley_order <- rev(river_levels)
p_comp <- ggplot(comp_fig, aes(percent, river_ID, fill = Material)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72, color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +

            aes(x = pos, label = sprintf("%.0f%%", percent)),

  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 1))
p_n <- ggplot(counts_fig, aes(N, river_ID)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.62, fill = "#8A8F96") +
```
