Three properties of trachyte account for this preference. First, size: trachyte cobbles (GM = `r f(gmT, 1)` mm) are significantly larger than sandstone (GM = `r f(gmS, 1)` mm) (*U* = `r f(size_U, 0)`, *p* `r fp(size_p)`), giving a larger initial volume from which to sustain prolonged reduction. Second, shape: `r f(trach_tabular_pct, 1)`% of trachyte cobbles are tabular and `r f(trach_irreg_pct, 1)`% irregular, these angular forms offer the acute natural edges and flat surfaces from which removals can be struck. Third, fracture properties: in thin section the trachyte has a porphyritic texture, with euhedral tabular to prismatic K-feldspar phenocrysts (c. 0.3–5.0 mm, c. 1–10% of the rock) set in a groundmass of K-feldspar microlites, chlorite or altered mafic minerals and magnetite, together with about 50% devitrified glass, forming a intersertal texture (\[\[Fig. X\]\]). A groundmass of this kind is likely to promote regular conchoidal fracture and hence sharp, continuous edges, while the crystalline fraction may give the material greater mechanical strength, and so greater durability in use, than a wholly glassy rock.

The advantage of trachyte therefore lies less in its availability than in what it affords: cobbles large and angular enough to be knapped, in a material whose texture combines predictable fracture with resistance to edge broken. These are the properties on which prolonged resharpening depends, and they are the same properties that the Quina system is understood to require.

## Characterising the Quina retouch products

### Techno-typological features

The `r n_scraper` Quina scrapers from the surface collections are consistent with the Quina technological concept in each of its three dimensions: in the blanks selection, in the retouch strategy, in the ramification (@tbl-retouch-products).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-retouch-products
#| tbl-cap: "Metric and reduction attributes of the Quina scrapers and the resharpening flakes from the surface collections. Not every attribute could be measured on every specimen: the platform attributes are recorded only on those that retain the platform of the blank, and GIUR on all but one scraper. The retouch attributes apply to the scrapers alone and the exterior platform angle to the resharpening flakes alone."

# one row per attribute; d = decimals for mean/SD, ds for the order statistics
row_num <- function(label, x, d = 1, ds = d) {
  x  <- as.numeric(x); x <- x[is.finite(x)]
  qs <- unname(quantile(x, c(.25, .75)))
  data.frame(Attribute = paste0(IND, label),
             mn  = f(mean(x), d), sd = f(sd(x), d),
             med = f(median(x), ds),
             iqr = paste0(f(qs[1], ds), "–", f(qs[2], ds)))
}
# panel heading, keeping the two classes of retouch product apart
row_head <- function(label, n_total) {
  data.frame(Attribute = sprintf("**%s** (*n* = %d)", label, n_total),
             mn = "", sd = "", med = "", iqr = "")
}

retouch_products_tbl <- bind_rows(
  row_head("Quina scrapers", nrow(q)),
  row_num("Length (mm)",    q$Length,    1),
  row_num("Width (mm)",     q$Width,     1),
  row_num("Thickness (mm)", q$Thickness, 1),
  row_num("Mass (g)",       q$Mass,      1),
  row_num("Platform depth (mm)", q$Platform_depth, 1),
  row_num("Platform width (mm)", q$Platform_width, 1),
  row_num("IPA (°)",             q$IPA,            1),
  row_num("Retouch generations", q$Ave_RG,    2),
  row_num(variable_labels[["N_Scar"]], q$N_Scar, 1, ds = 0),
  row_num("GIUR",                q$Ave_GIUR,  2),
  row_num("Edge angle (°)",      q$Edge_Angle, 1),
  row_num("Retouched perimeter", q$Retouch_length_index, 2),
  row_head("Resharpening flakes", nrow(rfl)),
  row_num("Length (mm)",    rfl$Length,    1),
  row_num("Width (mm)",     rfl$Width,     1),
  row_num("Thickness (mm)", rfl$Thickness, 1),
  row_num("Mass (g)",       rfl$Mass,      1),
  row_num("Platform depth (mm)", rfl$Platform_depth, 1),
  row_num("Platform width (mm)", rfl$Platform_width, 1),
  row_num("IPA (°)",             rfl$IPA,            1),
  row_num("EPA (°)",             rfl$EPA,            1))

knitr::kable(retouch_products_tbl, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
             col.names = c("Attribute", "Mean", "SD", "Median", "Q1–Q3"))
```

[Blank selection.]{.underline} Quina flaking yields thick flakes with markedly asymmetric cross-sections, detached by invasive percussion from cores worked on alternating plan-secant surfaces, and it is the volume held in such a blank that permits the successive stages of edge maintenance that follow \[Bourguignon 1997; Turq 1992\]. The blanks used here carry the attributes that this strategy produces. Most scrapers retain cortex to some degree (*n* = `r cortex_bearing_n`, `r f(cortex_bearing_pct, 1)`%), and where cortex survives it lies most often on a lateral margin (*n* = `r lateral_n` of `r cortex_bearing_n`, `r f(lateral_pct, 1)`%), opposite the retouched edge, forming a thick back. Some were made directly on cortical flakes, with cortex covering most of the dorsal face (*n* = `r primary_n`, `r f(primary_pct, 1)`%); among specimens without cortex, a latral thick back usually formed by previous removals (*n* = `r nocortex_n`, `r f(nocortex_pct, 1)`%). The asymmetric distribution of volume is therefore present whether or not the original surface of the cobble survives. These are not ordinary flakes that happened to be retouched, but blanks carrying a reserve of volume that were selected by knappers.

Platform observations point the same way. In all, `r plat_n` Quina scrapers (`r f(plat_pct, 1)`%) retain the platform of the original blank, and these are characteristically wide and oblique, with a median platform depth of `r f(pd_median, 1)` mm (Q1–Q3 = `r f(pd_q1, 1)`–`r f(pd_q3, 1)` mm) and a mean IPA of `r f(ipa_mean, 0)`° (*SD* = `r f(ipa_sd, 1)`°); both follow from the invasive percussion by which thick blanks are removed by plan-secant flaking. Plain platforms predominate (*n* = `r plain_n`, `r f(plain_pct, 1)`%), with cortical (*n* = `r natural_n`, `r f(natural_pct, 1)`%) and dihedral platforms (*n* = `r dihedral_n`, `r f(dihedral_pct, 1)`%) less common. Four of the dihedral specimens are *talons lisses à pan*, on which the platform preserves parallel removal scars running approximately orthogonal to the axis of percussion. Few though they are, these carry the most direct information in the assemblage about the reduction strategy behind the blanks: a platform of this kind records a surface that had itself previously served as a flaking surface, which is what the alternating plan-secant exploitation.

[Edge maintenance.]{.underline} The most distinctive feature of a Quina scraper is that the edge was sustained through successive episodes that follow a regular rythum. Retouch usually begins with convex removals and shifts as reduction proceeds towards concave removals, the two alternating across the life of the Quina scraper \[Bourguignon 1997; Peresani et al. 2024\]. That sequence is clearly expressed in this assemblage. Quina scrapers carry a mean of `r f(rg_mean, 2)` retouch generations (*SD* = `r f(rg_sd, 2)`), with a mean of `r f(cxs_mean, 1)` convex scars (*SD* = `r f(cxs_sd, 1)`) and `r f(cvs_mean, 1)` concave scars (*SD* = `r f(cvs_sd, 1)`) per specimen. Convex scars are concentrated in the first generation, concave scars in the second and third. The imbalance between the two, better than four concave removals for every convex one, is the quantitative signature of an edge maintained far beyond its initial production.

Two measures quantify how far that process was carried. The GIUR has a median of `r f(giur_median, 2)` (Q1–Q3 = `r f(giur_q1, 2)`–`r f(giur_q3, 2)`), indicating that retouch commonly extended into the zone of maximum blank thickness; the proportion of the perimeter retouched has a median of `r f(rli_median, 2)` (Q1–Q3 = `r f(rli_q1, 2)`–`r f(rli_q3, 2)`), consistent with the thick back retained on most specimens. A minority were worked more extensively across the whole piece, among them the triple scrapers and *limaces*. Mean edge angle is `r f(ea_mean, 1)`° (*SD* = `r f(ea_sd, 1)`°). Because the angle produced by the final generation alone cannot be isolated, what we measured is the angle of the edge as a whole, and this is better read as an index of cumulative reduction than as a direct measure of function [@linQuinaRetouchDoes2021]; edge angle shows significant positive correlation with GIUR (ρ = `r f(ea_giur["rho"], 2)`, *p* `r fp(ea_giur["p"])`), with the proportion of the perimeter retouched (ρ = `r f(ea_rli["rho"], 2)`, *p* `r fp(ea_rli["p"])`) and with the number of retouch generations (ρ = `r f(ea_rg["rho"], 2)`, *p* `r fp(ea_rg["p"])`) (@fig-edge-angle-reduction), which supports that reading.

```{r}
#| label: fig-edge-angle-reduction
#| fig-cap: "Scraper edge angle against the three other measures: proportion of the perimeter retouched, GIUR, and number of retouch generations. Each panel gives the Spearman ρ and its p-value; The dashed line represents an ordinary least-squares linear fit, shown only as a visual guide to the direction of the relationship."
#| fig-width: 5.9
#| fig-height: 2.44

# port of scripts/figures/edge_angle_reduction_figure.R
set.seed(2226)
focal_ea    <- "Edge_Angle"
corr_vars   <- c("Retouch_length_index", "Ave_GIUR", "Ave_RG")
corr_labels <- c(Retouch_length_index = "Retouched perimeter",
                 Ave_GIUR = "GIUR", Ave_RG = "Retouch generations")
fmt_p_math  <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "italic(p) < 0.001",
                                  sprintf("italic(p) == %.3f", p))

quina_ea <- read_excel(sc_path, sheet = "Quina scraper") |>
  mutate(across(all_of(c(focal_ea, corr_vars)), as.numeric))
spearman_one <- function(v) {
  pair <- quina_ea |> select(all_of(c(focal_ea, v))) |> drop_na()
  ct <- suppressWarnings(cor.test(pair[[focal_ea]], pair[[v]], method = "spearman", exact = FALSE))
  data.frame(Variable = v, rho = unname(ct$estimate), p_value = ct$p.value)
}
results_ea <- do.call(rbind, lapply(corr_vars, spearman_one))
results_ea$p_value <- p.adjust(results_ea$p_value, "bonferroni")   # one family of three

long_ea <- quina_ea |> select(all_of(c(focal_ea, corr_vars))) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(corr_vars), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") |>
  filter(!is.na(.data[[focal_ea]]), !is.na(Value)) |>
  mutate(Variable = factor(Variable, levels = corr_vars),
         x_plot = if_else(Variable == "Ave_RG", Value + runif(n(), -0.11, 0.11), Value))
labels_ea <- results_ea |>
  mutate(Variable = factor(Variable, levels = corr_vars),
         label = sprintf("rho == %.2f * ',' ~ %s", rho, fmt_p_math(p_value)))

fig_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E6E8EB", linewidth = 0.3),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = "#202124", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5),
        axis.ticks = element_line(color = "#202124", linewidth = 0.3),
        axis.ticks.length = unit(2, "pt"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 9), axis.text = element_text(color = "#303238", size = 8),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#202124", size = 8.5),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#E8E8E8", color = NA),
        plot.background = element_rect(color = NA, fill = "white"),
        panel.background = element_rect(color = NA, fill = "white"))

ggplot(long_ea, aes(y = .data[[focal_ea]])) +
  geom_smooth(aes(x = Value), method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE,
              color = "#6BA8CE", fill = "#CBDCEA", linewidth = 0.6, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(x = x_plot), color = "#565693", alpha = 0.5, size = 1.4, shape = 16) +
  geom_text(data = labels_ea, aes(x = -Inf, y = Inf, label = label), parse = TRUE,
            hjust = -0.08, vjust = 1.35, size = 2.5, color = "#202124", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ Variable, scales = "free_x", ncol = 3, labeller = as_labeller(corr_labels)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.14))) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.06)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Edge angle (°)") +
  fig_theme + theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank())
```

Within this common scheme the Quina scrapers vary typologically: `r styp_n["Single"]` of them (`r f(styp_p["Single"], 1)`%) carry retouch on a single edge, `r styp_n["Double"]` (`r f(styp_p["Double"], 1)`%) on two, and `r styp_n["Multi"]` (`r f(styp_p["Multi"], 1)`%) on three or more, and their attributions across Bordes' type list are given in @tbl-bordes-typology. Since every specimen conforms to the Quina retouch, this variation is more plausibly a matter of knappers adjusting to the blanks in front of them than evidence of distinct technological concept [@hiscock2007].

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bordes-typology
#| tbl-cap: "Attribution of the surface Quina scrapers within Bordes' type list, grouped by type family. Percentages are of the whole assemblage. The triple scraper is not a type of Bordes' list and is entered without a number."

# Bordes attribution as recorded, tidied: internal double spaces closed up, and
# the two orderings of the straight/convex double scraper merged, these being
# one type in Bordes' list rather than two.
bordes <- gsub("\\s+", " ", trimws(as.character(q$Bordes_typology)))
bordes[bordes == "Double convex-straight scraper"] <- "Double straight-convex scraper"

# the type list in Bordes' order: recorded label -> family, type number, short label
bordes_key <- tribble(
  ~family,                          ~no,  ~short,            ~recorded,
  "Simple scrapers",                "9",  "straight",        "Single straight scraper",
  "Simple scrapers",                "10", "convex",          "Single convex scraper",
  "Simple scrapers",                "11", "concave",         "Single concave scraper",
  "Double scrapers",                "12", "straight",        "Double straight scraper",
  "Double scrapers",                "13", "straight–convex", "Double straight-convex scraper",
  "Double scrapers",                "15", "biconvex",        "Double convex scraper",
  "Double scrapers",                "16", "biconcave",       "Double concave scraper",
  "Double scrapers",                "17", "convex–concave",  "Double convex-concave scraper",
  "Convergent and déjeté scrapers", "18", "straight",        "Straight convergent scraper",
  "Convergent and déjeté scrapers", "19", "convex",          "Convex convergent scraper",
  "Convergent and déjeté scrapers", "20", "concave",         "Concave convergent scraper",
  "Convergent and déjeté scrapers", "21", "déjeté",          "Déjeté scraper",
  "Transverse scrapers",            "22", "straight",        "Straight transverse scraper",
  "Transverse scrapers",            "23", "convex",          "Convex transverse scraper",
  "Transverse scrapers",            "24", "concave",         "Concave transverse scraper",
  "Other forms",                    "25", "inverse",         "Inverse scraper",
  "Other forms",                    "29", "alternate",       "Alternate scraper",
  "Other forms",                    "28", "bifacial",        "Bifacial scraper",
  "Other forms",                    "—",  "triple",          "Triple scraper",
  "Other forms",                    "8",  "limace",          "Limace")
bordes_fam <- tribble(
  ~family,                          ~no_range,
  "Simple scrapers",                "9–11",
  "Double scrapers",                "12–17",
  "Convergent and déjeté scrapers", "18–21",
  "Transverse scrapers",            "22–24",
  "Other forms",                    "")
# a label recorded outside the key would drop specimens from the table
stopifnot(setequal(unique(bordes), bordes_key$recorded))

bordes_key$n <- vapply(bordes_key$recorded, function(l) sum(bordes == l), integer(1))
pc <- function(x) f(100 * x / length(bordes), 1)

bordes_tbl <- bind_rows(lapply(bordes_fam$family, function(fm) {
  k <- bordes_key[bordes_key$family == fm, ]
  bind_rows(
    data.frame(Type = sprintf("**%s**", fm),
               no = bordes_fam$no_range[bordes_fam$family == fm],
               n = sum(k$n), pct = pc(sum(k$n))),
    data.frame(Type = paste0(IND, k$short), no = k$no, n = k$n, pct = pc(k$n)))
})) |>
  bind_rows(data.frame(Type = "**Total**", no = "", n = length(bordes), pct = f(100, 1)))

knitr::kable(bordes_tbl, row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
             col.names = c("Bordes type", "No.", "*n*", "%"))
```

[Ramification sequence.]{.underline} The resharpening flakes (*n* = `r rf_n`) support the reading of the retouch just described and, at the same time, document the third dimension of the Quina system. They are characteristically flat and oval in plan with an arched profile, and the proximal part of their dorsal face preserves scars of previous Quina retouch; their platforms are shallow (mean PD = `r f(rf_pd_mean, 1)` mm, *SD* = `r f(rf_pd_sd, 1)` mm), as marginal percussion produces. Their EPAs average `r f(epa_mean, 1)`° (*SD* = `r f(epa_sd, 1)`°), compared with a mean edge angle of `r f(ea_mean, 1)`° on the Quina scrapers. Although this difference approached significance (Welch's *t* = `r f(welch_t, 2)`, *df* = `r f(welch_df, 1)`, *p* `r fp(welch_p)`), its magnitude was small, with a Cohen's *d* of `r f(cohd, 2)` (95% CI: `r f(cohd_lo, 2)` to `r f(cohd_hi, 3)`), indicating only a limited separation between Quina scrapers' edge angle and resharpening flakes' EPAs. Since the EPA of a resharpening flake records the angle of the edge from which it was struck, the near identity of the two distributions is what would be expected if these flakes had been detached from Quina scrapers of the kind recovered alongside them; the small residual offset falls within the range that uneven sampling across surface localities would produce, and need not indicate a systematic difference in the angle at which edges were reworked.

Ramification extends beyond the maintenance of edges. Resharpening flakes carry cutting edges of their own and were therefore usable as struck, as use-wear analysis of such flakes at European Quina sites has confirmed [@delpiano2022; @claud2012]. Some Quina scrapers additionally bear "Clactonian notch" removals struck from the edge: broad, invasive scars whose corresponding resharpeninhg flakes are larger, and which are therefore themselves candidates for further modification [@peresani2023]. Material already in hand was thus drawn on repeatedly, first to restore a working edge and then to yield fresh blanks from the tool itself.

### Technological consistency

[Consistency with Longtan.]{.underline} The surface Quina scrapers cannot be distinguished from the excavated Quina scrapers at Longtan (*n* = `r ltq_n`), while both are clearly separated from the non-Quina scrapers (*n* = `r lto_n`) that serve as a control. In the technological space, PERMANOVA finds no difference between the two Quina groups (*R*² = `r f(tc_scltq_R2, 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(tc_scltq_F, 2)`, *p* `r fp(tc_scltq_p)`), whereas each differs from the non-Quina scrapers with an order of magnitude more explained variance (*R*² = `r f(min(tc_nonq_R2), 2)`–`r f(max(tc_nonq_R2), 2)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(min(tc_nonq_F), 1)`–`r f(max(tc_nonq_F), 1)`, *p* `r fp(tc_nonq_p)` in both cases) (@fig-technological-consistency).

```{r}
#| label: fig-technological-consistency
#| fig-cap: "Technological consistency of surface Quina scrapers with the excavated Longtan Quina scrapers, against Longtan non-Quina scrapers as a control, on six technical variables. (A) PCA of the z-scored technical space, with convex hulls, group centroids, variable loadings, and marginal histograms of the PC1 and PC2 scores by group. (B) Per-variable distributions with pairwise post-hoc brackets (ns / * / ** / *** / ****)."
#| fig-width: 5.9
#| fig-height: 8.07

# port of scripts/figures/statistic_figures.R (Fig. TC); reads the `tc` object
# assembled in the results-analysis chunk above.
group_colors <- c(SC_Quina = "#E07C90", LT_Quina = "#E6C25C", LT_Ordinary = "#6BA8CE")
group_labels <- c(SC_Quina = "Surface Quina", LT_Quina = "Longtan Quina",
                  LT_Ordinary = "Longtan non-Quina")
# variable_labels and variable_labels_bare come from _analysis.R, so that the
# six variables are named the same way here, in the tables below and in the
# supplementary material

fig_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E6E8EB", linewidth = 0.3),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = "#202124", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5),
        axis.ticks = element_line(color = "#202124", linewidth = 0.3),
        axis.ticks.length = unit(2, "pt"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 9), axis.text = element_text(color = "#303238", size = 8),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#202124", size = 8.5),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#E8E8E8", color = NA),
        legend.title = element_blank(), legend.text = element_text(size = 8.5),
        legend.key = element_blank(), plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        plot.background = element_rect(color = NA, fill = "white"),
        panel.background = element_rect(color = NA, fill = "white"))

scores   <- tc$pca_scores
loadings <- tc$pca_loadings
vexp     <- tc$var_explained
centroids <- scores |> group_by(Group) |> summarise(cx = mean(PC1), cy = mean(PC2), .groups = "drop")
hulls <- scores |> group_by(Group) |> filter(n() >= 3) |>
  group_modify(function(g, k) { h <- chull(g$PC1, g$PC2); bind_rows(g[h, ], g[h[1], ]) }) |> ungroup()
arrow_mult <- 0.85 * min(max(abs(scores$PC1)) / max(abs(loadings$PC1)),
                         max(abs(scores$PC2)) / max(abs(loadings$PC2)))
arrows_df <- loadings |> mutate(x = PC1 * arrow_mult, y = PC2 * arrow_mult,
                                Label = variable_labels_bare[Variable])
EXP_X <- expansion(mult = 0.20); EXP_Y <- expansion(mult = 0.10)

p_a <- ggplot(scores, aes(PC1, PC2, color = Group)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.3, color = "grey55") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.3, color = "grey55") +
  geom_polygon(data = hulls, aes(fill = Group, group = Group), alpha = 0.12, color = NA) +
  geom_path(data = hulls, aes(group = Group), linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.65) +
  geom_point(size = 1.1, alpha = 0.7, shape = 16) +
  geom_point(data = centroids, aes(cx, cy, fill = Group), shape = 21, color = "#5A5F66",
             size = 2.4, stroke = 0.6, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_segment(data = arrows_df, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = x, yend = y),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.075, "cm"), type = "open", angle = 22),
               linewidth = 0.22, color = "#5A5F66", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_text_repel(data = arrows_df, aes(x = x, y = y, label = Label),
               size = 2.2, color = "#3A3D42", bg.color = "white", bg.r = 0.12,
               segment.color = "grey55", segment.size = 0.2, min.segment.length = 0.2,
               box.padding = 0.35, point.padding = 0.1, max.overlaps = Inf, seed = 2226,
               inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = group_colors, labels = group_labels) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = group_colors, labels = group_labels) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = EXP_X) + scale_y_continuous(expand = EXP_Y) +
  labs(x = sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%%)", vexp[1]), y = sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%%)", vexp[2])) +
  fig_theme +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(), legend.position = "inside",
        legend.position.inside = c(0.995, 0.995), legend.justification = c(1, 1),
        legend.background = element_rect(fill = alpha("white", 0.85), color = NA),
        legend.margin = margin(2, 4, 2, 2), legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.key.height = unit(8, "pt")) +
  guides(fill = "none", color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 1.6, alpha = 1), ncol = 1))

marg_theme <- theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA), plot.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0))
p_mx <- ggplot(scores, aes(PC1, after_stat(density), fill = Group, color = Group)) +
  geom_histogram(position = "identity", alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.25, bins = 26) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = group_colors) + scale_color_manual(values = group_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = EXP_X) + scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  marg_theme + guides(fill = "none", color = "none")
p_my <- ggplot(scores, aes(y = PC2, after_stat(density), fill = Group, color = Group)) +
  geom_histogram(position = "identity", alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.25, bins = 22) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = group_colors) + scale_color_manual(values = group_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = EXP_Y) + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  marg_theme + guides(fill = "none", color = "none")

p_b <- ggplot(tc$variable_long, aes(Group, Value)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(color = Group), width = 0.3, height = 0, size = 0.8, alpha = 0.5, shape = 16) +
  geom_boxplot(color = "black", fill = NA, width = 0.6, linewidth = 0.45, outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 16, size = 1.4, color = "black") +
  stat_pvalue_manual(tc$posthoc_brackets, label = "p.adj.signif", y.position = "y.position",
     tip.length = 0.012, bracket.size = 0.3, label.size = 2.5, color = "#202124") +
  facet_wrap(~ Variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3, labeller = as_labeller(variable_labels)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = group_colors, labels = group_labels) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = group_labels) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.12))) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  fig_theme + theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1, size = 7.5)) +
  guides(color = "none")

top_row <- (p_mx + labs(tag = "A") + theme(plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))) +
  plot_spacer() + p_a + p_my +
  plot_layout(design = "AB\nCD", widths = c(5, 1), heights = c(1, 5.5))
top_row / (p_b + labs(tag = "B")) + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.5))
```

The control group is what makes this result interpretable. A non-significant difference is not enough by itself evidence of similarity: it may equally reflect variables too blunt to separate anything, or a sample too small to detect what is there. Because the same six variables separate Quina from non-Quina scrapers with relative higher *R*², they are demonstrably capable of resolving technological differences of the kind at issue here. What this establishes is not that the two groups are identical, which no test can show, but that any difference between them is far smaller than the difference that distinguishes Quina from non-Quina scrapers work.

The univariate results follow the same pattern. None of the six variables differs between the two Quina groups, while every one of them differs between each Quina group and the non-Quina scrapers (@fig-technological-consistency). Agreement therefore holds not only in the multi-dimension technological space but in each of its component measures.

Consistency of this concerns the position of group centroids, and two assemblages could share a centroid while differing in how widely they vary around it. PERMDISP shows that they do not. The mean distance to centroid is almost the same in the two Quina groups (`r f(pd_scq, 2)` and `r f(pd_ltq, 2)`; *F* = `r f(permdisp_scltq_F, 2)`, *p* `r fp(permdisp_scltq_p)`), whereas the non-Quina scrapers are less dispersed (`r f(pd_lto, 2)`) and differ significantly from both (*F* = `r f(min(permdisp_nonq_F), 1)`–`r f(max(permdisp_nonq_F), 1)`, *p* `r fp(permdisp_nonq_p)` in each case). Here again the control group establishes that the analysis can detect a real difference in dispersion where one exists, so that the absence of such a difference between the Quina groups is not a matter of sensitivity. The univariate dispersion tests agree: neither the KL-MSLRT nor the Fligner–Killeen tests detect any difference in variability between the two Quina groups (@tbl-dispersion-tests), and every dispersion ratio has a confidence interval containing one.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dispersion-tests
#| tbl-cap: "Univariate dispersion of the surface Quina scrapers against the Longtan Quina scrapers. Each family is summarised by the dispersion measure appropriate to its scale of measurement and tested by the corresponding procedure; the ratio is surface over Longtan, so that one denotes equal dispersion, and its interval is a bootstrap percentile interval. The statistic is the MSLRT for the coefficient of variation and the Fligner–Killeen chi-squared elsewhere."

# disp_labels comes from _analysis.R: the six variable_labels plus the three
# raw dimensions that enter this comparison alone
disp_heads <- c(CV      = "Coefficient of variation (CV\\*), KL-MSLRT",
                bounded = "Median absolute deviation, Fligner–Killeen",
                count   = "Fano factor, Fligner–Killeen")
# 3 decimals below one, 2 above, so that the CV and the Fano factor read alike
fd <- function(x) ifelse(abs(x) < 1, f(x, 3), f(x, 2))

disp_fmt <- bind_rows(lapply(names(disp_heads), function(fam) {
  d <- disp_tests[disp_tests$family == fam, ]
  bind_rows(
    data.frame(Variable = sprintf("**%s**", disp_heads[[fam]]),
               sc = "", lt = "", ratio = "", stat = "", p = ""),
    data.frame(Variable = paste0(IND, disp_labels[d$variable]),
               sc = fd(d$sc), lt = fd(d$lt),
               ratio = sprintf("%s (%s–%s)", f(d$ratio, 2), f(d$lo, 2), f(d$hi, 2)),
               stat = fd(d$stat), p = sub("^= ", "", vapply(d$p, fp, character(1)))))
}))

knitr::kable(disp_fmt, row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
             col.names = c("Variable", "Surface", "Longtan", "Ratio (95% CI)",
                           "Statistic", "*p*"))
```

These results are not driven by the material belongs to Longtan surface collections. Repeating the analyses with the surface specimens collected from within the area of the site removed leaves them unchanged. The two Quina groups remain indistinguishable both in centroid position (*R*² = `r f(sens_perm_scltq_R2, 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(sens_perm_scltq_F, 2)`, *p* `r fp(sens_perm_scltq_p)`) and in dispersion (*F* = `r f(sens_scltq_F, 2)`, *p* `r fp(sens_scltq_p)`), while both remain separated from the non-Quina scrapers in centroid position (*R*² = `r f(min(sens_perm_nonq_R2), 3)`–`r f(max(sens_perm_nonq_R2), 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(min(sens_perm_nonq_F), 1)`–`r f(max(sens_perm_nonq_F), 1)`, *p* `r fp(sens_perm_nonq_p)`) and significantly more dispersed than them (*F* = `r f(min(sens_nonq_F), 1)`–`r f(max(sens_nonq_F), 1)`, *p* `r fp(sens_nonq_p)`). The agreement documented here therefore reflects the surface collections as a whole rather than a single locality or a local peculiarity of sampling.

Taken together, in centroid position and in dispersion alike, the surface Quina scrapers and the excavated Quina scrapers from Longtan cannot be told apart on measurements that readily separate both from other retouched scrapers at the same site. They are most economically understood as the products of a single technological concept.

[Landscape structure.]{.underline} Technological variation is not structured by position in the landscape. Across the `r n_localities` localities that yielded measurable Quina scrapers, no landscape variable accounts for an appreciable share of the variation in the six technological measures: assemblage size (*R*² = `r f(ls_size["R2"], 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(ls_size["F"], 3)`, *p* `r fp(ls_size["p"])`), basin (*R*² = `r f(ls_basin["R2"], 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(ls_basin["F"], 3)`, *p* `r fp(ls_basin["p"])`), distance to the nearest channel (*R*² = `r f(ls_dist["R2"], 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(ls_dist["F"], 3)`, *p* `r fp(ls_dist["p"])`), and height above that channel (*R*² = `r f(ls_height["R2"], 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(ls_height["F"], 3)`, *p* `r fp(ls_height["p"])`). These low *R*² indicate that landscape variables had little explanatory power for technological variation in Quina scrapers, provide no evidence for a structured spatial influence.

One weak pattern nevertheless runs in a direction worth noting. All six technological measures correlate positively with distance to the nearest channel (Spearman's ρ = `r f(min(ls_dist_rho), 2)`–`r f(max(ls_dist_rho), 2)`; @tbl-distance-correlations), so that Quina scrapers from localities further from a channel tend to be thicker and more heavily reduced. The direction is the one predicted by work on the European Quina, where prolonged reduction are more pronounced at localities without ready access to abundant raw materials [@turq2000; @hiscock2009]. Two qualifications limit what can be made of this. No individual correlation reaches significance at this sample size, and the six measures are not independent of one another: edge angle covaries with GIUR, with the proportion of retouched edge and with the number of retouch generations (Section 4.2.1; @fig-edge-angle-reduction), so that the concordance of six coefficients does not amount to six independent confirmations. We therefore record the pattern as consistent with an established expectation, and as a hypothesis for landscape-scale work with larger samples, rather than as a demonstrated gradient.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-distance-correlations
#| tbl-cap: "Spearman rank correlation of each technological measure with distance to the nearest present-day channel. The unit is the locality, not the specimen: each locality that yielded measurable Quina scrapers is represented by the median of those scrapers, and the count of localities is given in the text. The interval on ρ is a bootstrap percentile interval over localities; adjusted *p* is the Bonferroni adjustment across the six tests."

ls_fmt <- data.frame(
  Measure = unname(variable_labels[ls_dist_cor$variable]),
  rho = f(ls_dist_cor$rho, 2),
  ci  = sprintf("%s to %s", f(ls_dist_cor$lo, 2), f(ls_dist_cor$hi, 2)),
  p   = sub("^= ", "", vapply(ls_dist_cor$p, fp, character(1))),
  pbh = sub("^= ", "", vapply(ls_dist_cor$p_adj, fp, character(1))))
ls_fmt <- ls_fmt[order(-ls_dist_cor$rho), ]

knitr::kable(ls_fmt, row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
             col.names = c("Measure", "ρ", "95% CI", "*p*", "Adjusted *p*"))
```

Across the study area, Quina scraper production in essentially the same way, regardless of the basin in which a locality occurs, its elevation above the channel, its distance from water, or the size of the assemblage it has yielded. Such homogeneity under contrasting landscape conditions is not unexpected but is precisely the pattern predicted for a consistently maintained technological system. The absence of landscape structuring should therefore be interpreted not as a lack of detectable variation, but as evidence for the repeated application of a shared technological concept across the region.

# Discussion

The Quina material from these two basins is the product of a single technological concept, which we refer to as the Quina Valley. Three lines of evidence converge on that conclusion. In raw material economy, the surface collections and the excavated assemblage at Longtan alike show a strong preference for trachyte, and that preference holds across the study area even though the gravel bars themselves vary significantly in composition from valley to valley. In technology, the scrapers display the diagnostic attributes of the Quina system: thick, asymmetric blanks with a back formed by cortex or by earlier removals; successive generations of retouch; the rhythmic alternation of convex and concave removals; and the continued production of resharpening flakes, some of which were used or reworked in turn. In their distribution across the landscape, neither technological characteristics nor raw material selection varies systematically with basin, height above the channel, distance to water or assemblage size. What the surface collections record, in other words, is not a scatter of superficially similar pieces but the repeated application of one way of working stone across a defined region.

Longtan is therefore no longer a single case. Its technological attribution has been debated: Bourguignon et al. (2025) observed that morphological resemblance need not imply cultural affinity, suggested that the blank production at Longtan might represent a variant of discoid technology, and expressed reservations about its dating and depositional context; Ruan et al. (2025) responded on techno-economic grounds, on the systematic differences from discoid reduction, and on the chronological and taphonomic evidence. Whatever the outcome of that exchange, a single site is limited in what it can carry. The contribution of the present study is to show that the same way of working stone recurs: across several valleys and several terrace levels in two basins, assemblages appear that agree with Longtan in raw material selection, in blank selection, in the manner of retouch and in the degree to which tools were reduced. These surface collections have no independent age control, and none is claimed for them. What their recurrence establishes is distributional rather than chronological: the Quina system in East Asia is documented at a regional scale, and no longer rests on the evidence of one excavated site.

Quina-style artefacts are not confined to this region. Comparable material has been reported from Dahe in Fuyuan, Yunnan, and Baicaoping in Liangshan, Sichuan, in southwestern China, and from Sanlongdong in Chifeng, Inner Mongolia, and Xinmiaozhuang in Yangyuan, Hebei, in the north \[\]. Most of these assemblages have not been analysed technologically, and whether they represent the Quina system or Quina retouch alone remains open. They are best treated for the moment as leads rather than as established occurrences. The pattern documented here is of a different kind: within the Hengduan Mountains, the Quina system is a recurrent and identifiable regional entity, and the scattered reports elsewhere in China suggest that its distribution in East Asia may prove wider still.

Whether the same technology in two regions implies any connection between the people who made it is a question the evidence cannot settle, and the more productive line is to ask what problem the technology solved. In Europe that problem is reasonably well understood. The prey on which Quina foragers depended were partitioned by topography rather than distributed evenly, reindeer occupying the ground between uplands and plain in a landscape of plateaux dissected by deep valleys, other species holding lower or more sheltered positions \[Delpech 1996\], so that movement was scheduled rather than opportunistic \[Delagnes and Rendu 2011\]. Foragers moving on such a schedule faced two problems at once: staying equipped while away from sources of stone, and not knowing in advance which tasks a given season and location would present. The three dimensions of the Quina system answer them in turn, in a reserve of volume that travels, an edge that can be restored without recourse to new stone, and a tool that can yield fresh edges of a different kind as needs change \[Hiscock et al. 2009\].

The setting on the southeastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau is not the European one, but it is likely to have posed a problem of the same structure. The regional monsoon record places the occupation at the transition from MIS 4 to MIS 3, when a recovering monsoon was repeatedly interrupted, and the pollen record at Longtan registers a local shift towards more open vegetation across the same interval \[Ruan et al. 2025\]; in relief of this amplitude a valley-floor pollen spectrum integrates several altitudinal belts, so that shift is better read as a relative trend than as a measure of how open the ground immediately around the site had become. What can be said about the structure of such a landscape comes from its modern counterparts. Dry-hot valleys of the Jinsha drainage today carry a strongly seasonal, rain-shadowed climate in which annual evaporation greatly exceeds rainfall, and in which surface water is concentrated onto the valley floors, where groundwater draining from the flanking uplands sustains the rivers \[Li et al. 2025\]; their vegetation is zoned by altitude, from savanna on the valley floors through transitional formations to forest on the surrounding heights \[Jiang et al. 2024\]. It is the topographic partitioning rather than the particular vegetation that is likely to have persisted: whatever the detailed palaeo-configuration, water and forage in a valley system of this relief would have been distributed unevenly with respect to elevation rather than uniformly across the terrain.

Both landscapes were open, and in that respect the comparison is unremarkable: openness alone is compatible with many regimes of resource distribution, including some that place no premium on mobility. What the two settings share is more specific. In each, the resources on which foragers depended were organised seasonally and partitioned by relief, by the topographic separation of plateau, valley and plain in southwestern France \[Delpech 1996\] and by the altitudinal zonation of water and forage here, so that they could not be obtained from any single location, but had to be met where and when they occurred. The difference lies in what produced that structure, glacial aridity in one case and monsoon seasonality in the other, and in the stone that was available to work, flint against trachyte; it does not lie in the structure itself. One term in the argument is untested. In the European sequence it runs from prey structure through mobility to technology and rests on faunal assemblages; no fauna has been analysed from the Quina Valley, so the mobility to which the technology is here related is inferred from the landscape rather than observed in it.

A shared problem of this kind provides a mechanism for convergence, and would allow two regions with no contact between them to arrive at technological solutions that are functionally alike. The Quina Valley is on this reading a techno-economic adaptation to a landscape whose resources had to be reached by moving through it. Diffusion cannot be ruled out, however. Quina technology in the western Old World is closely associated with Neanderthals, and the boundaries of their range continue to be redrawn, so the question of origin is better left open at this stage than closed by the argument that is presently most economical.

The Quina Valley bears on a longer-standing question about the East Asian Middle Palaeolithic. The conventional view held that lithic technology in the region was stable across the Palaeolithic and that no phase corresponding to the western European Middle Palaeolithic could be recognised. Levallois and discoid reduction reported at Guanyindong (c. 170–80 ka), Lingjing (c. 125–90 ka) and Jinsitai (c. 47–35 ka) have made that position increasingly difficult to hold \[\], and the Quina system at Longtan added a further technology to the picture. The present study shows that this is not an isolated occurrence but a way of working stone applied repeatedly across a region, and it offers a frame of reference for the assemblages elsewhere in China where Quina-like retouch has been reported but not yet analysed.

Four limitations qualify these results. The surface collections have no independent age control, so the recurrence documented here is a spatial pattern rather than a demonstrated contemporaneity; the shared technological concept, however, holds whether or not the assemblages are of one age. Cores were not analysed and blank production is inferred from the attributes of the blanks themselves, so the first of the three dimensions rests on indirect evidence, while the other two are documented directly and in quantity. No local palaeoclimate record is available for the Binchuan Basin, and the regional setting is inferred from the Heqing sequence, which is treated throughout as context rather than as a local proxy. Most consequentially, no faunal assemblage from the Quina Valley has been analysed, so the mobility and subsistence patterns to which the technology is here related are inferred rather than observed: in the European sequence the argument runs from prey structure through mobility to technology, and here the middle term is untested. Further excavation at Tianhuadong, and the recovery of primary-context assemblages in the Binchuan Basin, would supply the cores, the absolute ages and the faunal record that surface material cannot.
